bookTitle: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)

facts.topic: Put-Call Parity Formula for European Options on Non-Dividend-Paying Stock
facts.statement: Put-Call Parity establishes that for a European call option (c) and a European put option (p) with the same strike price (K), maturity date (T), and non-dividend-paying underlying stock (S_0), the pricing relationship is c + K*e^(-rT) = p + S_0, where K*e^(-rT) is the present value of the strike price discounted at the continuously compounded risk-free rate r.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Put-Call Parity defines a fundamental relationship between the price of a European call option (c) and a European put option (p) having the same strike price (K), maturity date (T), and underlying stock (S_0) paying no dividends

facts.topic: Put-Call Parity Replication Proof via Portfolio A and Portfolio B
facts.statement: Put-Call Parity is proven by constructing two portfolios at time t = 0: Portfolio A (1 European call c + cash of K*e^(-rT)) and Portfolio B (1 European put p + 1 share of underlying stock S_0). At expiration T, if S_T > K, Portfolio A pays (S_T - K) + K = S_T and Portfolio B pays 0 + S_T = S_T; if S_T <= K, Portfolio A pays 0 + K = K and Portfolio B pays K via put exercise. Because both portfolios yield the exact same terminal payoff max(S_T, K) in all states, the Law of One Price requires c + K*e^(-rT) = p + S_0.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: In both scenarios, both portfolios yield the exact same terminal payoff of \max(S_T, K) at time T. Under the no-arbitrage principle, two portfolios guaranteeing identical future payoffs in all market states must cost the same today.

payoffVsProfit.formulaProfit: max(S_T, K) - (c + K*e^(-rT)) = max(S_T, K) - (p + S_0)
payoffVsProfit.explanation: Both Portfolio A and Portfolio B produce an identical terminal payoff of max(S_T, K) at expiration T, so their initial investment costs (including option premiums c and p) must be equal at t = 0.

facts.topic: Fiduciary Call Arbitrage Steps When Call Side Is Overpriced (c + K*e^(-rT) > p + S_0)
facts.statement: When c + K*e^(-rT) > p + S_0, arbitrageurs execute a Fiduciary Call Arbitrage at t = 0 by: (1) selling/shorting the European call at c (+c), (2) buying the European put at p (-p), (3) buying 1 share of stock at S_0 (-S_0), and (4) borrowing K*e^(-rT) at the risk-free rate r (+K*e^(-rT)), locking in an upfront riskless profit of (c + K*e^(-rT)) - (p + S_0) > 0. At expiration T, whether S_T > K (short call exercised against trader for +K) or S_T <= K (long put exercised by trader for +K), the +K inflow exactly repays the -K loan obligation, netting 0 terminal cash flow.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: When the call option is overpriced relative to the put and stock, traders execute a Fiduciary Call Arbitrage

facts.topic: Reversal (Reverse Conversion) Arbitrage Steps When Call Side Is Underpriced (c + K*e^(-rT) < p + S_0)
facts.statement: When c + K*e^(-rT) < p + S_0, arbitrageurs execute a Reversal (Reverse Conversion) Arbitrage at t = 0 by: (1) buying the European call at c (-c), (2) selling/shorting the European put at p (+p), (3) short-selling 1 share of stock at S_0 (+S_0), and (4) lending/investing K*e^(-rT) at the risk-free rate r (-K*e^(-rT)), locking in an upfront riskless profit of (p + S_0) - (c + K*e^(-rT)) > 0. At expiration T, the invested cash grows to +K, which exactly pays the -K required to buy 1 share and close the short stock position via long call exercise (if S_T > K) or short put assignment (if S_T <= K).

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: When the call option is underpriced relative to the put and stock, traders execute a Reversal / Reverse Conversion Arbitrage

facts.topic: Business Snapshot 10.1: Merton's Model — Corporate Equity as a European Call Option
facts.statement: In Robert Merton's capital structure model (Snapshot 10.1), for a firm with total asset value V_T at time T and a single zero-coupon debt bond of face value D maturing at T, corporate equity is a European call option on the firm's assets (V) with strike price D and terminal payoff E_T = max(V_T - D, 0). If V_T > D, shareholders pay off debt D and retain V_T - D; if V_T <= D, shareholders default and walk away with 0 due to limited liability.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Equity is a European call option on the total assets of the firm (V) with a strike price equal to the face value of the firm's debt (D)

numericalDetails.context: Merton's structural model of corporate equity and limited liability at debt maturity T.

payoffVsProfit.explanation: Shareholders' terminal claim at debt maturity T is the call payoff max(V_T - D, 0) on total firm assets V_T above debt face value D.

facts.topic: Merton's Model — Corporate Debt as a Risk-Free Bond Plus a Short European Put
facts.statement: In Merton's model, the payoff to corporate debt holders at maturity T is min(V_T, D) = D - max(D - V_T, 0). Therefore, owning risky corporate debt is economically equivalent to holding a risk-free bond paying D at maturity T and simultaneously writing (shorting) a European put option on the firm's asset value V with strike price D.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Owning corporate debt is economically equivalent to holding a risk-free bond paying D and writing a European put option on the firm's value (V) with strike price D

formulaDetails.name: Merton Model Debt Holder Payoff
formulaDetails.latex: \text{Payoff to Debt Holders} = \min(V_T, D) = D - \max(D - V_T, 0)

facts.topic: Proof Why American Calls on Non-Dividend-Paying Stocks Are Never Exercised Early (C = c)
facts.statement: An American call option on a non-dividend-paying stock should never be exercised early before expiration, making its value identical to a European call (C = c), for three reasons: (1) Time Value of Money—waiting until T delays paying strike K, allowing the holder to earn risk-free interest on K over (T - t); (2) Downside Insurance Value—holding the call protects against the stock dropping below K between t and T, whereas early exercise exposes the holder to full stock downside below K; and (3) Dominance of Selling over Exercising—because C >= c >= S_t - K*e^(-r(T-t)) > S_t - K (for r > 0, T > t), the call's market price strictly exceeds its intrinsic value (S_t - K), so selling the call in the market always yields more than exercising early.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: For an American call option on a stock paying no dividends, C = c—meaning the American call has the exact same value as its European counterpart, and early exercise is never optimal

facts.topic: Early Exercise Conditions and Critical Barrier (S*) for American Puts
facts.statement: Unlike American calls, American put options on non-dividend-paying stocks can be optimal to exercise early when the stock price S_0 is sufficiently deep in the money (nearing 0, below a critical barrier S*). Because stock prices cannot fall below zero (S >= 0), the put's maximum payoff is capped at K; when S_0 is near 0, further downside is negligible and remaining insurance value is nearly zero, so the time value of money gained by receiving cash strike K immediately at time t and earning risk-free interest over (T - t) outweighs the forfeited insurance value, making immediate exercise value (K - S_0) exceed the value of continuing to hold the put.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Under these conditions, the time value of money on receiving K immediately outweighs any remaining insurance value

generalAssumptions: The underlying stock pays zero cash dividends over the life of the option contract (non-dividend-paying stock).
The risk-free interest rate r is positive (r > 0) and continuously compounded, allowing traders to borrow and lend freely at rate r.
Under the Law of One Price (no-arbitrage principle), any two portfolios that produce identical payoffs in every state at expiration T must have the exact same market price at time t = 0.
